title: Skills, commands and hooks
summary: A brilliant agent isn't the same as an expert one. Skills package your team's know-how into folders the agent loads only when needed. Commands save prompts you reuse. Hooks guarantee things happen every time. Here's what each is for, and how to grow them from real work.
takeaways: Skills are folders of know-how (a SKILL.md, plus scripts and references) that the agent loads only when relevant.
Only a skill's name and description sit in context up front, so you can have hundreds.
Grow skills from real work: repeated scripts, repeated mistakes, repeated workflows.
Commands are prompts you trigger yourself; hooks are scripts that run on every event, every time.
A prompt is a suggestion; a hook is a guarantee.
practices: Before starting a task, check whether an installed skill covers it and follow it.
When you write the same helper script twice, propose saving it into a skill.
Keep a skill's description specific about when to use it; keep the body short and link to references.
Respect hooks' results (formatters, linters, blocked commands); never work around a hook.

scenes.narration: A brilliant agent isn't the same as an expert one. This lesson is about turning your team's know-how into something agents can pick up, exactly when they need it.

params.title: Skills, commands and *hooks*
params.subtitle: Teach your agent your team's know-how.

scenes.narration: Barry Zhang from Anthropic uses a great analogy. You could ask a genius, like his colleague Mahesh, to do your taxes. But, he says, I don't want Mahesh to figure out the tax code from first principles. I need consistent execution from a domain expert. Skills are how you give an agent expertise.

params.text: I don't want Mahesh to figure out the 2025 tax code from first principles. I need *consistent execution* from a domain expert.
params.src: Don't Build Agents, Build Skills Instead · AI Engineer

scenes.narration: So what is a skill? Anthropic's answer: organized collections of files that package procedural knowledge for agents. In other words, they're folders. Inside, a SKILL file with a name and a description, plus any scripts, templates or reference docs it needs. Building one is like writing an onboarding guide for a new hire.

params.title: A skill is a folder
params.sub: “Like an onboarding guide for a new hire.”

scenes.narration: Here's what the file looks like. The front matter has a name and a description, and the description matters most: it's how the agent decides when to use the skill. Then come the steps, including how to verify. Scripts are run, not read, so they don't cost context.

lines: description: Cut a release. Use when asked to release, ship or tag a version.
1. Run `scripts/bump_version.py` with major, minor or patch
3. Verify: `pnpm test && pnpm build` must pass

scenes.narration: The magic is progressive disclosure. At startup, the agent only sees each skill's name and description, a few dozen tokens. When a task matches, it reads the full file. Linked references and scripts are pulled in only as needed. Daisy Hollman calls a skill a lazy system prompt.

layers.label: Name + description
layers.sub: always loaded · a few dozen tokens

scenes.narration: Where do good skills come from? From real work. Anthropic noticed Claude writing the same styling script over and over, so they had it save the script inside a skill. Lauren Tan turns every failure mode she sees into a skill. And at Uber, teams asked Claude to read their past code reviews and write a review skill. You can simply ask your agent to write one.

items.sub: Lauren Tan: every failure mode → a skill
Uber: “read our past reviews, write a skill”

items.text: Just ask the agent to write it

scenes.narration: Commands are simpler. A slash command, or prompt file, is just a saved prompt you trigger yourself, like a review checklist or a weekly changelog. Skills are chosen by the agent when relevant. Commands are chosen by you.

params.text: A command is a *saved prompt* you trigger yourself.
params.sub: /review · /changelog · /new-endpoint — skills are picked by the agent, commands by you.

scenes.narration: Hooks are different again. They're scripts that run on agent events, like after every file edit, before every shell command, or when the agent stops. Use them for anything that must happen every single time: format the code, run the linter, block a dangerous command.

params.caption: Simplified. Exact formats differ between agents; check your tool's docs.

scenes.narration: Here's the key difference. An instruction in a prompt or a memory file is a suggestion. The model will usually follow it, but not always. A hook is a guarantee, because it's ordinary code that runs every time. Daisy Hollman adds that hooks scale well: they put nothing in the context unless they have something to say.

right.title: Hook
items: Silent unless it has something to say

scenes.narration: So which do you use when? Facts needed every session go in the memory file. Know-how needed only sometimes becomes a skill. Prompts you reuse become commands. Anything that must happen every time becomes a hook. And new abilities come from tools and CLIs.

Dan Shipper's team at Every calls this compounding engineering. Every feature should make the next one easier, by codifying what you learned into prompts, skills and commands. Do that consistently, and your setup gets better every week.

params.text: Every feature should make the *next one easier*.
params.sub: Compounding engineering: codify each lesson into prompts, skills and commands. — Dan Shipper, Every

scenes.narration: Quick check. You want your code formatted after every single edit the agent makes, without exception. What should you use? Tap your answer.

A hook that runs after each edit
params.explain: Instructions are suggestions. A hook is code that runs every time.

scenes.narration: Write your first skill from real work. This prompt has the agent find a workflow you repeat and turn it into a skill, with verification built in.

params.title: Try it with your agent
params.intro: Turn a repeated workflow into a skill:
params.prompt:
Look at our recent git history and this repo. Find a workflow we
repeat (adding an endpoint, a release, a migration...). Write it as
.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md: a precise name and description of
when to use it, the steps, and how to verify. Put scripts in scripts/.

scenes.narration: Recap. Skills are folders of know-how, loaded only when needed. Grow them from real work, or just ask the agent to write them. Commands are saved prompts. Hooks are guarantees. And every feature should make the next one easier. Next: git, your safety net.
